text: Your toddler's vocabulary is exploding, and they may learn several new words each week. Read together daily and name everything you see.
Two-word phrases like "big truck" or "want cookie" are typical at this age. Expand on their words by saying "Yes, that is a big red truck!"
Your toddler may start showing interest in potty training. Watch for signs of readiness like staying dry for longer periods or telling you when their diaper is wet.
Jumping with both feet off the ground is a milestone between 18 and 24 months. Try jumping together on a soft surface for practice.
Your toddler may line up toys, sort objects by color, or group similar items together. These early math skills are building naturally through play.
Parallel play, where your toddler plays alongside but not directly with other children, is the normal social stage at this age.
Your toddler can follow simple one-step directions and may be starting to understand two-step instructions like "pick up the ball and bring it to me." Practice during everyday routines.
Imaginative play is becoming more elaborate. Your toddler may create scenarios with toy figures, act out stories, or assign roles during play.
Your toddler may show a hand preference around this age, though it is normal for it to continue switching until age 3 or later.
Tantrums may increase as your toddler grapples with wanting independence but not yet having the skills to do everything alone. Stay calm and validate their feelings.
Your toddler may start recognizing themselves in photos and mirrors and use "me" and "mine." This self-awareness is a major cognitive leap.
Walking up and down stairs while holding the railing is a developing skill. Practice together and celebrate their growing confidence.
Your toddler may begin to show empathy, comforting a crying friend or offering a toy to someone who is sad. Acknowledge and encourage this kindness.
Simple shape puzzles with 4-6 pieces challenge problem-solving skills. Show your toddler how to turn pieces to find the right fit.
Your toddler can likely identify several body parts and may start counting objects, even if the numbers are not always in order.
Your toddler still needs one nap per day, usually 1-2.5 hours after lunch. Most children benefit from keeping this nap until at least age 3.
Toddlers need about 11-14 hours of total sleep per day. If bedtime battles are frequent, evaluate whether the schedule needs adjusting.
Stalling tactics at bedtime become more creative now. Set a clear routine with a defined endpoint, like "after two books, it is time for sleep."
If your toddler starts having nightmares, comfort them calmly and reassure them that they are safe. Nightmares are a normal part of cognitive development.
A toddler clock that changes color at wake-up time can help your child understand when it is OK to get out of bed.
Keep the crib as long as your toddler is not climbing out. Transitioning to a toddler bed too early often leads to more night wakings and bedtime resistance.
If your toddler skips a nap, move bedtime 30-60 minutes earlier to prevent overtiredness from snowballing into a rough night.
Consistency in your bedtime response matters more than the specific method you use. Choose an approach you can sustain and stick with it.
A predictable daily schedule with meals, nap, and bedtime at roughly the same times helps your toddler's body clock stay regulated.
Major transitions like a new sibling, moving, or starting preschool can disrupt sleep temporarily. Extra comfort and routine consistency help.
If your toddler is afraid of the dark, a dim red or warm nightlight can provide comfort without disrupting melatonin production.
A sleep regression around this age often coincides with language explosions, potty training, or the arrival of a new sibling. It typically resolves in 2-6 weeks.
Active play and outdoor time during the day genuinely improve sleep quality at night. A tired body leads to deeper, more restorative sleep.
Avoid using the bed or bedroom as a punishment spot. You want your toddler to associate their sleep space with comfort and safety.
If your toddler has transitioned to a bed and keeps getting up, calmly walk them back each time with minimal interaction. Consistency is key.
Your toddler can eat most of what the family eats now. Serve the same meals in toddler-appropriate portions and let them choose how much to eat.
Milk intake should be about {{16-24 ounces|475-710 ml}} (2-3 cups) per day. Too much milk fills the stomach and reduces appetite for nutrient-dense solid foods.
Whole milk is recommended for younger toddlers because the fat supports brain development. As your child grows, your pediatrician may suggest switching to low-fat milk when the time is right.
Offer three meals and 2-3 structured snack times daily. Grazing all day can reduce hunger at mealtimes and make nutrition less balanced.
Your toddler may go on food jags, eating only one food for days. Continue offering variety at every meal and don't short-order cook.
Make food fun by using cookie cutters on sandwiches, arranging food in colorful patterns, or serving meals on a special plate.
Your toddler is learning to use a fork and spoon more skillfully now. Expect some spills but praise the effort and growing independence.
Omega-3 fatty acids support brain development. Include foods like salmon, chia seeds, walnuts, or fortified eggs in your toddler's diet.
Encourage your toddler to drink water throughout the day, especially during active play. A small, easy-to-hold cup makes independent drinking easier.
If your toddler is still breastfeeding, the WHO supports continued breastfeeding up to 2 years and beyond. There is no need to stop if it works for both of you.
Avoid labeling foods as "good" or "bad" around your toddler. Use neutral language like "this food gives us energy" or "this is a sometimes food."
Let your toddler help set the table, pour water from a small pitcher, or choose between two healthy options. Involvement encourages better eating.
Don't give up on rejected foods. Research shows it can take 15-20 exposures before a toddler accepts a new food. Keep offering without pressure.
If your toddler drinks juice, limit it to {{4 ounces|120 ml}} per day of 100% fruit juice. Better yet, offer whole fruit and water instead.
Fiber from fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and beans helps prevent constipation, which is common in toddlers. Aim for about 19 grams per day.
Well-child visits during this stage include growth measurements, developmental screening, and possibly blood tests your pediatrician recommends based on your child's needs.
Your toddler should have a dental check-up every six months. The dentist can apply fluoride varnish to protect developing teeth.
Brush your toddler's teeth twice daily with a smear (grain-of-rice size) of fluoride toothpaste until age 3, then increase to a pea-sized amount.
If your toddler is not putting two words together by age 2, talk to your pediatrician about a speech evaluation. Early intervention is most effective.
The annual flu vaccine is recommended for all children over 6 months. Getting vaccinated helps protect your toddler and those around them.
Toddlers in group care may get 8-12 colds per year. Each cold strengthens their immune system. Contact your pediatrician for high fever or symptoms lasting more than 10 days.
Canine teeth and second molars typically come in between 16 and 33 months. Offer cold foods and teething toys for comfort during this period.
If you introduce screen time, choose high-quality programming and watch together with your toddler. Co-viewing helps them understand what they are seeing.
Help your toddler learn to wash their hands with soap for 20 seconds, especially before meals and after using the bathroom or playing outside.
If your toddler snores loudly every night or seems to stop breathing during sleep, mention it to your pediatrician. It could indicate enlarged adenoids.
Your toddler's eyes should be aligned by now. If you notice one eye crossing in or turning out, schedule an eye exam promptly.
Protect your toddler's skin with SPF 30+ sunscreen, a hat, and UV-protective clothing when outdoors. Reapply sunscreen every 2 hours.

Stuttering or repeating words is common between ages 2 and 5 as language develops faster than speech muscles can keep up. It usually resolves on its own, but mention it to your pediatrician if it persists beyond 6 months.
If potty training causes constipation, increase fiber and fluid intake and avoid pressuring your toddler. Stool withholding is common during this transition.
Ensure your toddler gets 600 IU of vitamin D daily through diet, fortified milk, or a supplement. Many toddlers do not get enough from food alone.
Encourage your toddler to draw circles and lines on paper. These are the building blocks of letter formation and develop hand control.
Build with larger interlocking blocks. Your toddler can create towers, bridges, and structures, developing spatial thinking and planning skills.
Play pretend store, restaurant, or doctor. This role-play develops language, social skills, and emotional understanding.
Splash in puddles, run through sprinklers, or play in a sandbox. Messy, sensory-rich outdoor play is essential for healthy development.
Tearing paper and playing with playdough build the hand strength needed for future scissor use. Closer to age 2, you can introduce child-safe scissors for early snipping practice.
Read books with simple storylines and ask your toddler questions: "What do you think happens next?" or "Can you find the cat?"
Musical instruments like drums, shakers, and xylophones teach rhythm, cause and effect, and creative expression.
Set up a simple obstacle course: crawl under a table, jump over a pillow, walk along a tape line on the floor. This builds planning and gross motor skills.
Play matching games with pictures or colors. Start with just 3-4 pairs and increase as your toddler's memory grows.
Painting with brushes, sponges, or fingers lets your toddler experiment with color and texture. Focus on the process, not the product.
Encourage climbing at the playground. Going up ladders, across bridges, and down slides develops courage, coordination, and risk assessment.
Play hide-and-seek around the house. Your toddler will squeal with delight and practice spatial memory, listening skills, and self-control.
Introduce counting during everyday activities: count steps as you climb them, crackers on the plate, or toys as you put them away.
Let your toddler help with gardening. Digging, watering, and watching plants grow teaches patience, responsibility, and nature connection.
Encourage your toddler to tell you about their drawings, even if they look like scribbles to you. Asking "tell me about your picture" builds narrative skills.
Your toddler can climb higher and reach further than ever. Re-evaluate your home for new hazards from their perspective regularly.
Keep your toddler rear-facing in the car seat as long as possible, ideally until they reach the seat's maximum weight or height limit. Rear-facing is the safest position for young children.
Teach your toddler basic water safety rules: never go near water without a grown-up, and always wear a life jacket near open water.
Popcorn, whole nuts, hard candy, and chunks of raw vegetables remain serious choking hazards for toddlers. Continue cutting food into small pieces.
Practice fire escape routes with your family. Show your toddler how to crawl low and go to a designated meeting spot outside.
If your toddler can open the front door, add a high chain lock or deadbolt they cannot reach. Toddlers can wander outside unsupervised in moments.
Teach your toddler their full name and begin working on your phone number. Use songs or repetition to make it fun and memorable.
Always check that playground equipment is age-appropriate and well-maintained. Look for openings that could trap a toddler's head or fingers.
Keep bathroom doors closed or use a toilet lock. Toddlers are fascinated by water and a toilet poses a drowning risk for a top-heavy child.
Review your car seat installation regularly. Ensure the harness is snug with the chest clip at armpit level and no bulky winter coats under straps.
Teach your toddler to sit while eating. Running or playing with food in their mouth significantly increases the choking risk.
Store sharp kitchen tools like knives, peelers, and scissors in a high drawer with a child lock. Your toddler can now open many lower drawers and cabinets.
If your toddler is transitioning to a bed, place the mattress low to the ground and use a bed rail. Remove hazards from the room they could access at night.
Driveway and parking lot safety is critical. Always hold your toddler's hand and check behind your vehicle before backing up. They are too short to be seen.
Check smoke and carbon monoxide detectors monthly and replace batteries at least once a year. A working detector is one of the simplest ways to protect your family.
